description: We are six friends from Uruguay: five developers and one storyteller. Axel, Kevin, Santiago, Bayron and Brandon built the core, the data pipeline, the harmonization and the app; Americo shaped the pitch, the film and the site.
summary: Two generations of NASA fire satellites, MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, record burning in ways that cannot be compared directly, so nobody has had one consistent picture of when and where burning happens. firecal harmonizes both records from NASA FIRMS into a single burning-activity calendar for any area the user draws: months across, years down. Every harmonized number carries an estimated uncertainty, so a month is called unusual only when it clears that band and is not just a change of sensor. The calendar can show hotspot counts or fire radiative power, finds the past seasons that most resemble the current one, exports a CSV, and keeps working with no signal in a region pinned beforehand. It runs in the browser at https://firecal.pages.dev/, over twenty years of all of Australia. It matters because the people who decide where to look for burning need to know how much to trust a number, not only the number.
details:
What it does. The user picks an area on a map, by drawing a rectangle or a polygon or by typing latitude and longitude bounds. The app shows the burning calendar for it, every month from November 2000 to December 2019: one cell per month and year on an accessible sequential color ramp, in two modes, hotspot count or total fire radiative power. It compares the current month with the historical median, shows the past seasons that look most like the one in progress, and downloads a CSV of what the search covers. After a region is pinned, all of it works with the network off. The hosted app has tiles for all of Australia; the map outlines that region, and an area outside it says it has no data yet and offers a way there, rather than showing numbers it does not have.

How it works. NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) are aggregated per cell and month. VIIRS counts are mapped to MODIS-equivalent counts per tile by quantile mapping, fitted on the years both sensors observed; the residuals over those years are the uncertainty shipped with every cell. The result is a set of static tile files. A single Rust core computes the series, the anomaly flag, the analog years and the CSV, and is compiled twice: native for the data pipeline and to WebAssembly for the browser. A test requires both builds to give identical bytes. The TypeScript interface only draws; every number on screen comes from the core. There is no backend, so the app is a static site and works offline. The interface is drawn by hand in code, in the same style and with the same drawing code as the film and the project's site, so the three read as one thing.

What sets it apart.

  1. Uncertainty on every number, and a month flagged only when it rises past the band and above every baseline year.
  2. Energy as well as counts: many small agricultural burns look different from a few large fires.
  3. Analog years: a picture of the seasons most like this one, compared by rank within the month, so quiet and busy regions are judged the same way.
  4. An offline field tool: the function that harmonized the archive runs in the browser, with no signal.

What we do not claim. A hotspot is a thermal anomaly seen from orbit, not a measured fire or a burned area. Harmonized counts are MODIS-equivalent and validated only on the overlap years. Analog years are history, not a forecast. The newest months come from near-real-time data and are provisional. Sigma adds cell errors as if they were independent, which is optimistic where neighbors share a bias, so the app says it is estimated.

Results we can state. All from pitch/numbers.md, where each has who measured it and what it does not show. Over south-east Australia, twenty years of public FIRMS records (16.6 million rows) were ingested in 7.3 seconds and harmonized into 230 months of tiles in a quarter of a second, on a laptop. Holding 2019 out of the calibration, raw VIIRS counted 12.5 times what MODIS counted, and harmonized VIIRS 0.77 times: close to MODIS from a gap of an order of magnitude, and low because 2019 went past anything the calibration had seen. The core flags November and December 2019 as unusual (December: 7,112 hotspots against a median December of 7) and finds 2009, 2001 and 2002 as the most similar past years; in the browser it answers that in under a millisecond, with no network. The same build over all of Australia writes 15 tiles of 230 months in under half a second; in the hosted app, December 2019 is flagged unusual in south-west Western Australia (384 hotspots) and in the Top End (505) as well. On the South America season of July and August 2026, the pipeline harmonized 24 complete 10° tiles in 0.06 seconds on a laptop, into 346 kilobytes of static files. In the fitted month, raw VIIRS saw 67,025 hotspots where MODIS saw 7,000; harmonized, VIIRS gives 7,000 (agreement by construction on the month it was fitted on; no held-out month yet). In the browser, the same Rust core answers an area query in about 13 microseconds over those tiles, and gives byte-identical results to the native build on 8,968 test calls. With the network off, a pinned region still answers, checked in Chrome on macOS, Windows and Linux on every change. Ingest read the whole public Uruguay archive, 97,392 rows, in 79 milliseconds.

Tools. Rust (a Cargo workspace, no third-party dependencies in the core crates), WebAssembly, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap's OpenStreetMap tiles, TerraDraw for drawing; Node for the tests and headless Chrome for the offline test; Cloudflare Pages to host the static site. The demo film was drawn as SVG in headless Chrome and encoded with Apple's AVFoundation.

What we hope to achieve. A calendar that any land or emergency manager can read, with the honesty to say when it is not sure.
